meta.name: ENT (Otolaryngology) Knowledge Base
meta.purpose: Structured reference data for a decision-support / educational chatbot. NOT a diagnostic device.
meta.disclaimer: This knowledge base is a curated clinical reference summary, not a substitute for professional medical judgement, examination, imaging, or laboratory testing. It is intended to assist recall and organize differentials for clinicians, students, and informed patients -- it must never be the sole basis for a diagnosis or treatment decision. Always correlate with clinical examination and local guidelines.
meta.last_reviewed_note: Content compiled from general standard otolaryngology teaching (e.g. Cummings Otolaryngology, Scott-Brown's, UpToDate-style summaries) at a general educational level. It has NOT been independently re-verified against current primary literature and may not reflect the newest guidelines -- verify against current sources before clinical use.
knowledge_sources: Cummings Otolaryngology: Head & Neck Surgery — Definitive ENT reference text
Scott-Brown's Otorhinolaryngology, Head and Neck Surgery — Comprehensive British reference
UpToDate-style Clinical Summaries — Evidence-based review format
Branchial Arch Embryology (Standard Medical Teaching) — Congenital anomaly development
AAO-HNS Clinical Practice Guidelines — Referral and management protocols
NICE Clinical Knowledge Summaries (UK) — Primary care ENT guidance
meta.compilation_note: Content compiled from general standard otolaryngology teaching at a general educational level. NOT independently re-verified against current primary literature.

conditions.name: Congenital Preauricular Sinus (Preauricular Pit/Fistula)
conditions.definition: A congenital epithelial-lined tract, usually located anterior to the crus of the helix, resulting from incomplete fusion of the first and second branchial (pharyngeal) arch hillocks (of His) during external ear development.
conditions.epidemiology: Prevalence varies widely by population, roughly 0.1-0.9% in most Western populations but up to 4-10% in some African and Asian populations. Can be unilateral or bilateral (bilateral cases have a higher association with other anomalies).
conditions.etiology: Failure of fusion of the hillocks of His during weeks 6-8 of embryogenesis, leaving a blind-ending epithelial tract that may branch and can extend close to the facial nerve and temporalis fascia.
associations: Can be part of Branchio-Oto-Renal (BOR) syndrome, especially if bilateral or with hearing loss/renal anomalies
symptoms: asymptomatic pit in front of the ear
occasional clear or mucoid discharge from the pit
signs: small dimple or pit anterior to the crus of the helix
may express mucoid material on gentle pressure
surrounding skin normal if uninfected
tract may be palpable as a cord-like structure
differential_diagnosis: First branchial cleft anomaly (different location/tract course)
Preauricular skin tag/accessory tragus (solid, not a tract)
investigations: Usually a clinical diagnosis, no imaging needed if uncomplicated
Renal ultrasound if bilateral pits, other syndromic features, or family history suggestive of BOR syndrome
Audiology screening if syndromic features or hearing concerns
MRI/fistulogram only if complex recurrent disease before revision surgery, to map tract extent

management.asymptomatic: No treatment required; reassurance and observation. Advise the family/patient to avoid manipulating or squeezing the pit.
management.infected_or_recurrent: Treat acute infection first (see Preauricular Sinus Cellulitis/Abscess entry), then consider elective complete surgical excision of the sinus tract once infection has resolved, since recurrence is common without full tract excision.
management.surgical_note: Surgical excision should remove the entire tract (which may branch) down to and including a cuff of perichondrium/cartilage if involved, to reduce recurrence; care must be taken near the temporal branch of the facial nerve.

complications: Perichondritis or auricular cartilage involvement if untreated infection spreads
red_flags: Signs of perichondritis (severe pain, erythema of the pinna cartilage)
conditions.when_to_refer: Refer to ENT for any recurrent or infected preauricular sinus, for elective excision after infection control, or if syndromic features (bilateral pits, hearing loss, renal anomalies, family history) are present.

conditions.name: Preauricular Sinus Cellulitis / Abscess (Infected Congenital Preauricular Sinus)
conditions.category: Ear - Infection (complication of congenital preauricular sinus)
conditions.definition: Acute bacterial infection of a congenital preauricular sinus tract and/or the surrounding soft tissue, ranging from superficial cellulitis to a discrete abscess.
conditions.etiology: Obstruction or trauma to the sinus tract allows bacterial entry; most commonly Staphylococcus aureus (including MRSA in some regions) and Streptococcus species; Proteus and anaerobes are also reported, particularly in recurrent/chronic cases.
risk_factors: Prior manipulation, squeezing, or piercing of the pit
Prior episodes of infection (recurrence is common)
Poor hygiene of the tract opening
symptoms: pain and tenderness anterior to the ear
redness and swelling around the preauricular pit
purulent or foul-smelling discharge from the pit
fever (more common if abscess or spreading cellulitis)
fluctuant swelling if abscess has formed
signs: localized erythema and induration around the sinus opening
tenderness on palpation
purulent discharge expressible from the pit
fluctuant, tender mass if abscess present
possible regional lymphadenopathy (preauricular/parotid nodes)
look for extension toward the pinna cartilage (risk of perichondritis)
differential_diagnosis: Perichondritis of the pinna (from other causes, e.g. piercing)
investigations: Primarily clinical diagnosis
Wound/pus swab for culture and sensitivity, especially in recurrent or non-resolving cases or if MRSA is a concern
Ultrasound of the soft tissue if abscess extent is unclear or to guide drainage
CT with contrast reserved for extensive, deep, or recurrent disease with suspected deeper extension

management.mild_cellulitis_no_abscess: Oral antibiotics covering Staphylococcus and Streptococcus (e.g. a first-generation cephalosporin or anti-staphylococcal penicillin per local guidelines and allergy status), warm compresses, and close follow-up. Consider MRSA coverage if local prevalence is high or risk factors present.
management.abscess_formation: Incision and drainage (or needle aspiration for smaller collections) plus antibiotics; pus should be sent for culture to guide/de-escalate therapy.
management.recurrent_or_after_infection_resolves: Elective complete surgical excision of the sinus tract is recommended once acute infection is fully settled, as incising through active infection increases recurrence and scarring risk. Excision should ideally be delayed several weeks after infection resolves.
management.important_principle: Avoid definitive tract excision during active infection/abscess when possible -- drain/treat the acute infection first, then plan elective excision.

complications: Perichondritis or chondritis of the auricular cartilage (serious, can cause cartilage destruction/cauliflower ear if untreated)
Scarring, and fistula recurrence if excision is incomplete
Rarely, spread to deeper structures (parotid space)
red_flags: Rapidly spreading erythema beyond the preauricular area
Severe pain out of proportion to exam findings
Signs of cartilage involvement (perichondritis) -- disproportionate pain, cartilage swelling
Immunocompromised patient or poorly controlled diabetes
conditions.when_to_refer: Refer urgently to ENT (or emergency care) if abscess formation, systemic symptoms/fever, suspected cartilage involvement, or if not responding to a course of appropriate oral antibiotics within 48-72 hours. Refer electively for tract excision once infection has resolved.

conditions.name: Acute Otitis Media (AOM)
conditions.definition: Acute inflammation and infection of the middle ear, typically following eustachian tube dysfunction after an upper respiratory tract infection.
conditions.etiology: Common pathogens: Streptococcus pneumoniae, non-typeable Haemophilus influenzae, Moraxella catarrhalis; viral URIs are frequently the preceding trigger.
signs: bulging, erythematous tympanic membrane
reduced or absent light reflex
reduced tympanic membrane mobility on pneumatic otoscopy
purulent discharge if TM perforated
differential_diagnosis: Otitis media with effusion (no acute signs of infection)
Mastoiditis (complication, not a differential per se)
investigations: Primarily clinical/otoscopic diagnosis
Tympanometry if diagnosis unclear
Culture of discharge only if persistent/recurrent or treatment failure

management.mild_or_watchful_waiting_candidates: Analgesia (paracetamol/ibuprofen); many guidelines support observation for 48-72 hours in well-appearing children over 2 years without severe symptoms.
management.antibiotics_indicated: First-line typically high-dose amoxicillin (or amoxicillin-clavulanate if recent antibiotic use, recurrent AOM, or concurrent conjunctivitis), per local guidelines and allergy status.
management.recurrent_disease: Consider ENT referral for tympanostomy tube evaluation if 3+ episodes in 6 months or 4+ in 12 months.

red_flags: High fever with severe systemic illness
Postauricular swelling/protrusion of the ear (suggests mastoiditis)
conditions.when_to_refer: Refer for recurrent AOM, treatment failure, suspected mastoiditis, or any intracranial complication signs.

conditions.name: Otitis Externa (Swimmer's Ear)
conditions.definition: Inflammation/infection of the external auditory canal skin, often due to bacterial or fungal infection, frequently precipitated by moisture or trauma.
conditions.etiology: Most commonly Pseudomonas aeruginosa and Staphylococcus aureus; fungal (otomycosis, e.g. Aspergillus, Candida) in a subset, especially after antibiotic ear drop use or in humid climates.
risk_factors: use of cotton buds/hearing aids/earplugs causing trauma
diabetes (risk factor for malignant/necrotizing otitis externa)
symptoms: ear pain, often severe, worse with movement of the tragus/pinna
aural fullness/hearing reduction if canal is swollen shut
signs: tenderness on tragal pressure or pinna traction (classic finding)
erythematous, edematous ear canal
debris/discharge in canal
canal may be too swollen to visualize tympanic membrane
investigations: Clinical diagnosis via otoscopy
Swab for culture in refractory, recurrent, or immunocompromised cases
CT/MRI and specialist referral if malignant otitis externa suspected

management.first_line: Topical antibiotic +/- steroid ear drops (e.g. a quinolone-based otic drop); keep the ear dry; aural toilet (gentle cleaning) if debris present.
management.severe_canal_swelling: An ear wick may be inserted to allow drops to penetrate a swollen canal.
management.fungal: Topical antifungal drops if otomycosis confirmed/suspected.
management.malignant_otitis_externa: Requires urgent ENT referral, IV antibiotics (typically anti-pseudomonal), and imaging -- this is a serious, potentially life-threatening skull-base osteomyelitis, mainly in diabetics/immunocompromised.

complications: Malignant otitis externa (skull base osteomyelitis) -- rare but serious
red_flags: Diabetic or immunocompromised patient with severe/refractory otitis externa (risk of malignant otitis externa)
Severe unrelenting pain, especially at night
conditions.when_to_refer: Refer if not improving after a full course of topical treatment, if malignant otitis externa is suspected, or if recurrent.

conditions.name: Cholesteatoma
conditions.definition: An abnormal, locally destructive growth of keratinizing squamous epithelium within the middle ear or mastoid, which can erode surrounding bone.
conditions.etiology: Can be congenital (behind an intact TM, no history of infection/perforation) or acquired (often from chronic negative middle ear pressure/retraction pocket, or implantation after trauma/surgery).
symptoms: chronic, often foul-smelling otorrhea unresponsive to standard drops
occasionally dizziness or facial weakness if advanced
signs: retraction pocket or perforation with visible keratin debris/white mass on otoscopy
granulation tissue
conductive hearing loss on tuning fork tests (Rinne negative, Weber lateralizes to affected ear)
differential_diagnosis: Chronic suppurative otitis media without cholesteatoma
investigations: Otoscopy/microscopy
Audiometry
CT temporal bone to assess extent of bony erosion before surgery

management.definitive: Surgical removal (mastoidectomy +/- tympanoplasty) is the mainstay -- cholesteatoma will not resolve with medical therapy alone and continues to erode bone if untreated.
management.medical_adjunct: Topical/oral antibiotics can control associated infection but do not treat the underlying disease.

complications: Intracranial spread: meningitis, brain abscess (rare but serious)
red_flags: Signs of intracranial infection (severe headache, neck stiffness, altered consciousness)
conditions.when_to_refer: All suspected cholesteatoma should be referred to ENT for assessment and likely surgery.

conditions.name: Acute Mastoiditis
conditions.definition: Infection extending from the middle ear into the mastoid air cells, usually a complication of inadequately treated or severe acute otitis media.
conditions.etiology: Same organisms as AOM (S. pneumoniae, H. influenzae, S. pyogenes, S. aureus).
symptoms: persistent ear pain and fever despite AOM treatment
signs: postauricular erythema, tenderness, and swelling
auricle pushed forward and down/outward
bulging TM on otoscopy
possible sagging of the posterior-superior ear canal wall
differential_diagnosis: Preauricular sinus infection (different location, more anterior)
investigations: Clinical diagnosis supported by otoscopy
CT temporal bone with contrast if complication or subperiosteal abscess suspected
Blood cultures if systemically unwell

management.core: IV antibiotics covering typical AOM pathogens, ENT involvement early; myringotomy +/- tympanostomy tube for drainage and culture.
management.abscess_or_complications: Mastoidectomy if subperiosteal abscess, treatment failure, or intracranial complication.

complications: Intracranial spread: meningitis, sigmoid sinus thrombosis, brain abscess
conditions.when_to_refer: Urgent ENT / emergency referral -- this is a potentially serious infection requiring prompt treatment.

conditions.name: Acute Rhinosinusitis
conditions.definition: Inflammation of the nasal and paranasal sinus mucosa lasting under 4 weeks, most often viral, occasionally with secondary bacterial infection.
conditions.etiology: Predominantly viral (rhinovirus, influenza, etc.); bacterial superinfection (S. pneumoniae, H. influenzae, M. catarrhalis) in a minority, typically after symptoms worsen after initial improvement ('double-worsening').
signs: tenderness over affected sinuses
purulent discharge on nasal exam
edematous nasal mucosa
investigations: Clinical diagnosis in most cases
Nasal endoscopy or CT sinuses reserved for chronic, recurrent, or complicated cases

management.viral_most_cases: Supportive: saline irrigation, analgesia, intranasal corticosteroids for symptom relief; antibiotics not indicated.
management.suspected_bacterial: Consider antibiotics if symptoms persist beyond 10 days without improvement, or severe symptoms (fever >39C, facial pain, purulent discharge) for 3-4 consecutive days, or 'double-worsening' pattern -- per local guidelines.

conditions.when_to_refer: Refer urgently if orbital or intracranial complication suspected; refer to ENT for recurrent/chronic disease.

conditions.name: Allergic Rhinitis
conditions.definition: IgE-mediated inflammation of the nasal mucosa triggered by inhaled allergens, either seasonal (e.g. pollen) or perennial (e.g. dust mite, pet dander).
signs: pale/boggy nasal turbinates
allergic shiners (infraorbital darkening)
nasal crease from repeated rubbing ('allergic salute')
differential_diagnosis: Rhinitis medicamentosa (from overuse of decongestant sprays)
investigations: Clinical diagnosis usually sufficient
Skin prick testing or specific IgE testing if allergen identification needed for immunotherapy planning

management.first_line: Intranasal corticosteroid sprays +/- oral or intranasal antihistamines; allergen avoidance where feasible.
management.refractory: Consider allergen immunotherapy for confirmed allergen-specific disease not controlled by medical therapy.

conditions.when_to_refer: Refer to allergy/ENT if refractory to standard therapy or for immunotherapy consideration.

conditions.name: Nasal Polyps (Chronic Rhinosinusitis with Nasal Polyps)
conditions.definition: Benign, edematous, inflammatory growths of the sinonasal mucosa, often bilateral, associated with chronic rhinosinusitis.
associations: Aspirin-exacerbated respiratory disease (Samter's triad: asthma, polyps, aspirin sensitivity)
Cystic fibrosis (especially unilateral polyps in children)
signs: pale, grey, grape-like masses visualized on anterior rhinoscopy or nasal endoscopy
bilateral in typical inflammatory polyps
differential_diagnosis: Inverted papilloma (unilateral, needs biopsy to exclude)
Antrochoanal polyp (unilateral, arises from maxillary sinus)
investigations: Nasal endoscopy
CT sinuses to define extent before surgery
Biopsy if unilateral or atypical features (to exclude malignancy)

management.medical: Intranasal (and sometimes short-course oral) corticosteroids as first-line.
management.surgical: Functional endoscopic sinus surgery (FESS) for those failing medical therapy or with significant obstruction.

complications: Recurrence after surgery, especially without ongoing medical therapy
red_flags: Unilateral polyp/mass -- must exclude malignancy or inverted papilloma
conditions.when_to_refer: Refer to ENT for endoscopic assessment; any unilateral nasal mass warrants urgent referral to exclude malignancy.

conditions.name: Epistaxis (Nosebleed)
conditions.definition: Bleeding from the nasal cavity, most commonly from Little's area (Kiesselbach's plexus) anteriorly in the nasal septum.
etiology: Nasal/sinus tumors (rare, consider if unilateral, recurrent, and in an older patient or associated with other red flags)
symptoms: bleeding from one or both nostrils
posterior bleeds may present with bleeding into the throat/hematemesis
signs: visible bleeding point on anterior rhinoscopy (usually Little's area) for anterior bleeds
posterior bleeds harder to visualize, often heavier and bilateral
differential_diagnosis: Nasal/sinonasal neoplasm if recurrent unilateral bleeding in an at-risk patient
investigations: Usually clinical
Coagulation studies/FBC if recurrent, severe, or on anticoagulants
Nasal endoscopy/imaging if recurrent unilateral bleeding to exclude a mass

management.first_aid: Sit upright, lean slightly forward, firm continuous pressure on the soft lower nose for 10-15 minutes, ice pack.
management.if_bleeding_point_visible: Topical vasoconstrictor + chemical cautery (e.g. silver nitrate) or electrocautery.
management.if_not_controlled: Anterior (+/- posterior) nasal packing; posterior bleeds or refractory cases may need ENT and possible arterial ligation/embolization.
management.review_medications: Review anticoagulant/antiplatelet therapy in consultation with the prescribing team; do not stop anticoagulation unilaterally without discussion.

red_flags: Bleeding not controlled with standard first aid after 20 minutes
Recurrent unilateral bleeding in an older patient (consider malignancy)
Bleeding diathesis or on anticoagulation with major bleed
conditions.when_to_refer: Refer/emergency care for uncontrolled bleeding, hemodynamic instability, or suspicion of an underlying mass/bleeding disorder.

conditions.name: Acute Tonsillitis / Peritonsillar Abscess (Quinsy)
conditions.definition: Acute tonsillitis is inflammation/infection of the palatine tonsils, viral or bacterial; peritonsillar abscess (quinsy) is a collection of pus between the tonsil capsule and the pharyngeal muscles, a complication of tonsillitis.
conditions.etiology: Tonsillitis: viral (most common, e.g. adenovirus, EBV) or bacterial (Group A Streptococcus most notable). Quinsy: usually polymicrobial, including Group A Strep and anaerobes.
symptoms: for quinsy: severe unilateral throat pain, trismus (difficulty opening mouth), muffled 'hot potato' voice, drooling
signs: tonsillar erythema/exudate
tender cervical lymphadenopathy
for quinsy: unilateral peritonsillar bulging, uvula deviated to the opposite side, trismus
investigations: Centor/McIsaac criteria to estimate probability of Group A Strep and guide antibiotic decisions
Throat/rapid strep swab where available
For quinsy: clinical diagnosis; needle aspiration is both diagnostic and therapeutic; CT with contrast if diagnosis unclear or deep neck extension suspected

management.bacterial_tonsillitis: Penicillin-based antibiotics (per local guidelines/allergy status) if bacterial cause likely per clinical scoring.
management.peritonsillar_abscess: Needle aspiration or incision and drainage, plus IV/oral antibiotics; ENT involvement recommended.
management.recurrent_tonsillitis: Consider ENT referral for tonsillectomy evaluation if recurrent episodes meeting criteria (e.g. 'Paradise criteria' region-dependent).

conditions.when_to_refer: Urgent ENT/emergency referral for suspected quinsy, airway compromise, or deep neck space infection signs.

conditions.name: Acute Laryngitis
conditions.definition: Inflammation of the larynx, most commonly due to a viral upper respiratory infection, causing hoarseness/voice change.
signs: erythematous, edematous vocal folds on laryngoscopy (if performed)
normal airway in typical viral cases
differential_diagnosis: Laryngeal malignancy (persistent hoarseness >2-3 weeks in a smoker/older adult -- red flag)
investigations: Usually clinical for acute short-duration hoarseness
Laryngoscopy if hoarseness persists beyond 2-3 weeks, or red flags present

management.acute_viral: Voice rest, hydration, humidification; avoid whispering (paradoxically strains the voice); resolves within 1-2 weeks typically.
management.reflux_related: Lifestyle modification, consider acid suppression if laryngopharyngeal reflux suspected.

complications: Chronic hoarseness if underlying cause not addressed
Vocal fold nodules with continued vocal abuse
red_flags: Hoarseness persisting more than 2-3 weeks, especially in smokers or those with significant alcohol use (exclude laryngeal malignancy)
conditions.when_to_refer: Refer to ENT for laryngoscopy if hoarseness persists beyond 2-3 weeks or any red flag features present.

conditions.name: Benign Paroxysmal Positional Vertigo (BPPV)
conditions.definition: The most common cause of vertigo, caused by displaced otoconia (calcium carbonate crystals) in the semicircular canals (most often posterior canal) triggering brief, intense vertigo with specific head movements.
symptoms: brief episodes of spinning vertigo (seconds, usually <1 minute) triggered by head position change, e.g. rolling over in bed, looking up
no hearing loss or tinnitus (distinguishing from Meniere's disease)
signs: positive Dix-Hallpike test showing torsional/upbeating nystagmus with latency and fatigability (posterior canal BPPV)
differential_diagnosis: Central causes of vertigo (stroke -- especially if other neurological signs present)
investigations: Dix-Hallpike maneuver is diagnostic for posterior canal BPPV
Supine roll test if lateral canal BPPV suspected
Imaging (MRI) only if atypical features or central cause suspected

management.first_line: Canalith repositioning maneuvers -- Epley maneuver for posterior canal BPPV is first-line and highly effective, often single-session.
management.adjunct: Vestibular rehabilitation exercises if recurrent or residual imbalance; vestibular suppressant medications generally not recommended for routine use as they can delay central compensation.

red_flags: Vertigo with focal neurological deficits, severe headache, or inability to walk (consider central/stroke etiology -- 'HINTS' exam by a trained clinician can help differentiate)
conditions.when_to_refer: Refer to ENT/audiovestibular specialist if diagnosis unclear, atypical nystagmus, or recurrent/refractory to repositioning maneuvers.

conditions.name: Tinnitus
conditions.definition: The perception of sound (ringing, buzzing, hissing) in the absence of an external auditory stimulus; a symptom rather than a single disease, with many possible underlying causes.
etiology: Age-related or noise-induced hearing loss (most common association)
Ototoxic medications (e.g. aminoglycosides, high-dose aspirin, some chemotherapy agents)
Vestibular schwannoma (acoustic neuroma) -- important to exclude if unilateral
Pulsatile tinnitus: vascular causes (e.g. AV malformation, glomus tumor, venous hum) -- warrants further workup
symptoms: pulsatile tinnitus (synchronous with heartbeat) is a distinct red-flag pattern
signs: often no abnormal findings on examination; assess for cerumen, TM abnormality, and perform hearing assessment
differential_diagnosis: Vestibular schwannoma (unilateral tinnitus + asymmetric hearing loss)
investigations: Audiometry in all persistent tinnitus cases
MRI internal auditory canals if unilateral tinnitus with asymmetric sensorineural hearing loss (to exclude vestibular schwannoma)
Further vascular imaging if pulsatile tinnitus

management.general: Treat underlying cause if identified (e.g. remove cerumen, review ototoxic medications); hearing aids can help if associated hearing loss present.
management.chronic_bothersome_tinnitus: Sound therapy/masking devices, cognitive behavioral therapy, tinnitus retraining therapy can help reduce distress; no universally curative pharmacological treatment exists.

red_flags: Unilateral tinnitus with asymmetric hearing loss (exclude vestibular schwannoma)
conditions.when_to_refer: Refer to ENT/audiology for persistent tinnitus, any unilateral tinnitus, or pulsatile tinnitus.

conditions.name: Obstructive Sleep Apnea (OSA) - Adult
conditions.definition: Repeated episodes of partial or complete upper airway obstruction during sleep, causing intermittent hypoxia and sleep fragmentation.
symptoms: witnessed apneas by a bed partner
signs: elevated BMI/neck circumference
crowded oropharynx (e.g. high Mallampati score, enlarged tonsils)
retrognathia
investigations: Polysomnography (sleep study) is the diagnostic gold standard, measuring the Apnea-Hypopnea Index (AHI)
Home sleep apnea testing for selected uncomplicated cases
Screening questionnaires (e.g. STOP-BANG, Epworth Sleepiness Scale) to guide referral

management.first_line: Weight loss, positional therapy, avoidance of alcohol/sedatives before sleep; CPAP (continuous positive airway pressure) is first-line for moderate-severe OSA.
management.alternatives: Mandibular advancement devices for mild-moderate OSA or CPAP-intolerant patients; surgical options (e.g. tonsillectomy/adenoidectomy in children with adenotonsillar hypertrophy, or various upper airway surgeries in select adults) depending on anatomy and severity.

complications: Motor vehicle accidents from daytime sleepiness
red_flags: Severe daytime sleepiness affecting driving safety
Uncontrolled hypertension/cardiac symptoms in the context of suspected OSA
conditions.when_to_refer: Refer to sleep medicine/ENT for polysomnography and management planning if OSA suspected clinically.

conditions.name: Sialadenitis (Salivary Gland Infection/Inflammation)
conditions.definition: Inflammation of a salivary gland (most often parotid or submandibular), which may be infective (bacterial or viral) or due to obstruction (sialolithiasis/stones).
etiology: Bacterial (often Staph aureus) -- typically associated with dehydration/reduced salivary flow, post-operative patients
Obstructive/calculus-related (sialolithiasis), more common in the submandibular gland due to viscous saliva and an uphill duct course
symptoms: painful swelling of the affected gland
pain worsened by eating (classic for obstructive/stone-related cases, as saliva flow increases)
purulent discharge from the duct opening if bacterial
signs: tender, swollen gland
erythema over the gland if infective
pus expressible from Stensen's (parotid) or Wharton's (submandibular) duct on gland massage
palpable stone along duct course in some cases
differential_diagnosis: Salivary gland tumor (usually painless, gradually enlarging)
investigations: Clinical exam with duct massage
Ultrasound to look for stones/abscess
CT if abscess or deep extension suspected
Sialography or CT/MR sialography for recurrent obstructive symptoms

management.acute_bacterial: Hydration, warm compresses, gland massage, sialogogues (e.g. sour sweets) to stimulate flow, antibiotics covering Staph aureus.
management.sialolithiasis: Conservative measures first; sialendoscopy or surgical removal of the stone/gland for persistent/recurrent obstruction.

red_flags: Airway compromise from floor-of-mouth swelling (Ludwig's angina, a surgical emergency)
Persistent painless mass (consider tumor, refer for further workup)
conditions.when_to_refer: Refer to ENT/maxillofacial for recurrent sialadenitis, suspected sialolithiasis needing intervention, or any suspicious mass.

conditions.name: Vocal Fold Nodules
conditions.definition: Benign, bilateral, symmetric callus-like lesions on the vocal folds at the junction of the anterior and middle thirds, resulting from chronic vocal abuse/misuse.
risk_factors: occupational voice use (teachers, singers, call center workers)
symptoms: reduced vocal range, especially for singers
signs: bilateral symmetric nodules at the junction of anterior 1/3 and posterior 2/3 of the vocal folds on laryngoscopy
an hourglass-shaped glottic gap on phonation
differential_diagnosis: Laryngeal malignancy (must exclude if risk factors/persistent hoarseness)
investigations: Laryngoscopy/stroboscopy for diagnosis and to assess vocal fold vibration

management.first_line: Voice therapy with a speech-language pathologist is first-line and often resolves nodules without surgery; address underlying vocal abuse and reflux if present.
management.surgical: Microlaryngoscopic surgical removal reserved for nodules persisting despite adequate voice therapy.

red_flags: Hoarseness >2-3 weeks in smokers/older adults without clear benign cause (exclude malignancy)
conditions.when_to_refer: Refer to ENT for laryngoscopy and voice therapy referral if hoarseness persists beyond 2-3 weeks.
